source.note: knowledge/disagreements.md point 9 identifies the combination both camps agree on: an ambition- or comparison-flavoured motive paired with thin evidence of readiness elsewhere. The second clause is broader here than at the steps below — it adds response_when_rough and widens the active_piloting branch to include 'try to react' — because Advance's framing ties the demand specifically to behaviour in turbulence, which is what those two questions measure. It still contains no hours clause; thermic hours gate separately and on their own evidence.

gates.message: The goals are fine — they're the reason people keep flying, and nobody should talk you out of them. One X-Alps pilot interviewed on exactly this calls the wish to achieve something the force that drives real progression. The gap is the groundwork underneath, and almost all of it is learnable on the wing you've got. That's what the suggestions below are about.

source.cites: Recommended handling: ambition itself is legitimate fuel (Guschlbauer via XC Mag's 'The Head Game', cited directly in knowledge/steps/mid-b-to-high-b.md) and must not be penalised alone; the concerning pattern is ambition paired with thin readiness. Seb Ospina via XC Mag is the counterpoint held alongside it: real readiness is demonstrated, not aspirational.
source.note: Only fires when the skills category is already below 55, which is why the message is framed around the groundwork rather than the ambition. Identical in structure to both steps below. Note that at this step 'longer_xc' is the NORMAL ambition for the class — the sources position it as a cross-country tier — so the gate's second clause is doing all the work, exactly as intended.

gates_deliberately_not_included.reason: No source gives a cumulative total-airtime figure for this boundary; all three give thermic-hours figures. Gating on a number nobody stated, when the sources agreed on a different number they did state, would be the wrong kind of precision. Scored at weight 5, and used only to narrow the second thermic gate. See meta.design_decisions 'v1-the-hours-gate-is-a-thermic-hours-gate'.

Gating at the figure itself was considered and rejected. knowledge/disagreements.md point 6 reduces the ~50-hour agreement from three sources to roughly two independent voices, and all three say 'roughly' or '50+'. The gates sit at under 10 unconditionally and at under 25 with thin total airtime; the 25-50 band is a Ready-blocker through scoring rather than a cap.
No source gives a flight count at this boundary at all. Scored at weight 3 on entirely unsourced bands, which is recorded in that question's disagreement_note rather than hidden.

No source gives a figure for time on a mid-B before a high-B. Flybubble's 150+ hours applies to a first B one rung down, and knowledge/disagreements.md point 6 records Flybubble's own articles disagreeing with each other on it. Scored at weight 7; the behavioural version is asked directly by wing_limiting_evidence.

knowledge/steps/mid-b-to-high-b.md records that no source gives a ground-handling test for this step and that BHPA's own Pilot Rating Scheme page was checked directly and does not name ground handling at all. knowledge/disagreements.md point 11 says explicitly not to invent a numeric test where none exists. Scored at weight 7 plus 3, and not even a Ready-blocker.

Flybubble recommends regular proactive practice at this stage but frames it as practice to be doing, not a precondition. Promoted from 'not even a blocker' at the step below to a Ready-blocker here, which is as far as the evidence reaches. Scored at weight 10 and drives two high-priority suggestions.

'I mostly soar rather than thermal' is an untested answer, not a weak one, so it is handled as a Ready-blocker through unevidenced_core_checks rather than a cap — but with no stated-plans exemption at this step, unlike the two below. See thresholds.ready.unevidenced_core_checks.exemptions_deliberately_empty.

Two industry sources describe speed-bar technique at this step and neither sets a standard to clear. Weight doubled to 6 and 'never used it' scored down to 0.25, which is the proportionate response to descriptive rather than prescriptive material.

Carried forward from config/scoring/a-to-low-b.json's v2 removal of exactly this gate and config/scoring/low-b-to-mid-b.json's v1 decision not to reinstate it: an injury or reserve ride is not reliably about wing-class readiness. Scored 0.0 on a weight-12 psychological question. Not re-litigated here.

BRIEF.md requires SIV to be optional context only and knowledge/disagreements.md point 1 agrees. knowledge/steps/mid-b-to-high-b.md records that no source gates on SIV here, and that it is notably absent even from Flybubble, who start requiring it one rung up. Bonus-only, capped at 2 points, can never subtract.

knowledge/disagreements.md point 7 records this was searched for specifically across every source and found nowhere, and knowledge/steps/mid-b-to-high-b.md re-checked it at this boundary — where sources do discuss turbulent thermic air in general terms — and still found nothing falsifiable. Not asked, not scored, not gated.

knowledge/steps/mid-b-to-high-b.md records that no source ties an XC distance or site count to this boundary; the figures appear one rung up and come from pilot-rating ladders rather than wing-class sources. knowledge/disagreements.md point 14 adds Joy Paragliding arguing against distance as a proxy for wing readiness at all. Not asked.

gate_behaviour.rule: Any fired gate caps the recommendation at Not yet, regardless of score. The numeric score is still shown, with the gate reasons listed above it.
gate_behaviour.evaluation_order: Gates are evaluated first and short-circuit: if any gate fires, the recommendation is Not yet and the threshold rules (category floors, critical_check_floor, unevidenced_core_checks) are not evaluated or reported. This keeps the explanation short and specific rather than piling on reasons.
gate_behaviour.tone_rule: Gate messages state what to work on and why, never that the pilot is unsuitable or has failed. Required by BRIEF.md's safety framing and by docs/design-context.md, which requires a 'not yet' to land as a legitimate, successful result of using the tool.

source.cites: "Hard gates: some answers ... cap the result at 'Not yet' regardless of total score."
source.note: This rubric has 11 gates against 9 at A to low-B and 8 at low-B to mid-B, so the cap of 3 shown reasons does real work here: a genuinely unready pilot can trip four or five. The gates array is ordered so that the specific, actionable ones (training status, thermic hours, currency, launches, collapse control, instructor advice) sit above the two combination gates about motive, which read worse when they arrive first. tests/personas/mid-b-to-high-b/06 trips three and is the one to read for whether the stacking reads as a telling-off.

rule_messages.purpose: Pilot-safe copy for the threshold rules, so a pilot held at Nearly ready or pushed to Not yet by a rule gets the same explicit 'here's what's holding this back' as a pilot held by a hard gate. Gates carry their copy on gate.message. Built in from v1 at this step, as at low-B to mid-B, rather than added in a later pass as at A to low-B.

lookup.engine_output: app/upgrade/lib/scoreEngine.ts returns ScoreResult.firedRules as an array of strings in one of two shapes: '<rule_id>' (only 'conservative_backstop' today) or '<rule_id>:<question_id_or_category>' (everything else).
lookup.structure: Two flat maps. 'by_rule' is keyed by the EXACT fired-rule string, so no parsing or templating is needed at render time. 'fallback_by_rule_id' is keyed by the part before the colon, and exists only so a future question added to critical_check_floor.questions (or a future answer added to unevidenced_core_checks.answers) can never render a missing message.
algorithm: 3. if still not found: render nothing for that rule. Never render the raw fired-rule string, a rule id, or a question id to a pilot.
lookup.render_as: Each entry has a plain prose 'message' string, exactly like gate.message, intended for the same 'What's holding this back' card and the same paragraph treatment. There is deliberately no per-message heading field: rules can fire together, and two headings in one card reads badly.
lookup.division_of_labour_with_suggestions: Every answer band that can trip a threshold rule also triggers a suggestion in config/suggestions/mid-b-to-high-b.json, and both appear on the same result screen. The split is: the rule message says WHY this one answer is holding the result and what the standard is; the suggestion says HOW to move it. The pairs are thermic_airtime/build_thermic_hours, flying_frequency/improve_currency, wing_limiting_evidence/wing_hasnt_limited_you_yet, thermal_turn_control/thermal_skills_drill, reading_the_day/reading_the_day_drill, active_piloting/active_piloting_drill, collapse_experience/post_collapse_support, collapse_practice/collapse_practice_now, reserve_familiarity/reserve_practice, response_when_rough/nerves_are_not_the_problem, and unevidenced_core_checks:thermal_turn_control/thermalling_untested. If any of those suggestions is retired, re-read the paired message — a 'there's a suggestion below' pointer with nothing below it is the failure mode to watch for.
lookup.multiplicity: critical_check_floor breaks on its first failing question, so at most ONE 'critical_check_floor:*' string can appear in firedRules, and the question it names is the first failure in thresholds.ready.critical_check_floor.questions order, not necessarily the worst one — which is why that list is deliberately ordered most-to-least step-specific. Same for unevidenced_core_checks. The two category-floor rules are independent and can both appear. Gates and rules are mutually exclusive: gates short-circuit, so firedRules is always empty when firedGates is non-empty.
lookup.internal_fields: The 'source' block on each entry is provenance for the owner and reviewer only. Only 'message' is ever rendered.

display.order: The order the engine emits them, which is already roughly most-to-least specific: category floors, then critical_check_floor, then unevidenced_core_checks, then conservative_backstop.
display.why_two_and_not_three: gate_behaviour.max_gate_reasons_shown is 3, but several rules can fire together on the Nearly ready path, and these are softer and more overlapping reasons than gates. Nearly ready means 'close' — listing five things reads as a telling-off and contradicts the result. Two keeps it specific; the suggestions list carries the rest.
display.tone_rule: Same rule as gate_behaviour.tone_rule. Step-specific addition: messages here MAY name the ~50-hour thermic figure, because it is genuinely corroborated and pilots benefit from knowing the number — but they must attribute it ('the guidance keeps landing on', 'the published figure is') rather than state it as this tool's own bar, and must never claim three independent sources agree. knowledge/disagreements.md point 6.

source.cites: The brief requires the result to be transparent and rule-based rather than a black box, and requires the 'Not yet' framing to be a legitimate result rather than a failure.
source.note: docs/design-context.md's safety guard is the binding constraint on the two not_yet_category_floor messages. No wording from that document, and none of its terminology, appears in any message here.

critical_check_floor:thermic_airtime.message: One thing is holding this back, and it's the best-evidenced check on the whole page: thermal hours specifically. The published guidance for this step keeps landing on around 50 of them, and you're under about 25. Worth being clear about what this isn't — it isn't a comment on your flying, and ridge or coastal hours aren't wasted hours. It's that this particular class of wing is sold and described as a thermic, cross-country wing, so thermic time is the experience it's asking for. One source does count ridge soaring toward it, at roughly half value; we've taken the stricter reading of that, because the other two sources don't. The suggestions below are about how to add the hours without making a project of it.

source.cites: Hamerton via Cross Country Magazine (expert), Flybubble (industry) and 406 Paragliding (industry) all land on roughly 50 hours of thermic flying; Hamerton alone offers roughly 100 hours of ridge soaring as an alternative. Advance, Gin, Nova and Flybubble all position the class for cross-country and turbulent thermic air.
source.note: Reached by the 10_25 band only: under_10 is caught earlier by a gate, and 25_50 scores 0.6 and passes. The ridge sentence is load-bearing honesty — it tells a coastal pilot their result turns on a choice between disagreeing sources rather than on a settled fact, per knowledge/disagreements.md point 2. This is the message tests/personas/mid-b-to-high-b/03 renders.

critical_check_floor:flying_frequency.message: One thing is holding this back: flying about once a month. That's the only check on this page where the three big manufacturers of high-end B wings all say the same thing in their own words — these aren't wings for occasional pilots, and they want you current rather than just experienced. There's no agreed number behind that, so it holds the result rather than capping it. Two or three times a month, in whatever conditions you can get, changes this answer and several others with it.

source.cites: Nova (manufacturer): "not suitable for beginners and occasional pilots". Advance and Gin via Flybubble (manufacturer via retailer): reserved for pilots who are naturally talented or very current.
source.note: Only 'about once a month' reaches this rule: 'no flying at all in three months' and 'less than monthly with a thin year' are caught earlier by gates. The message says 'no agreed number' deliberately — the manufacturer sources are qualitative, and paragliding24.ch's 50-80 annual-hours figure is flagged as uncorroborated in knowledge/disagreements.md point 6.

critical_check_floor:wing_limiting_evide.message: One thing is holding this back, and it's the single most-agreed point in the guidance for this step: by your own account, your current wing hasn't clearly been the thing stopping you yet. Four voices say the same thing in different words — including two manufacturers writing about their own high-end B wings — that this is a wing you move onto because you've run out of the one you've got. None of that is a criticism, and it's a good problem to have: it usually means there's performance still sitting in your current wing waiting to be collected, which is the cheapest kind there is. The suggestion below has a concrete way to test whether that's true.

source.cites: Seb Ospina via XC Mag (industry/expert) on consistently maxing out the current wing; Advance and Gin via Flybubble (manufacturer via retailer) warning against aspirational purchases; Hamerton via Cloudbase Mayhem 72 (expert) on matching equipment to demonstrated ability.
source.note: Reached by 'not really' and 'I've wondered but couldn't point to a flight'. A pilot answering 'not really' alongside thin currency or thin thermic hours is caught earlier by the 'aspirational_rather_than_demonstrated' gate, so this rule mostly fires for the otherwise-strong pilot, which is why the tone is explicitly non-critical.

critical_check_floor:thermal_turn_contro.message: One thing is holding this back: thermalling that works but isn't yet under your control — wide turns, losing the core. That carries more weight here than one rung down, because every source that puts a number on this step counts thermal hours specifically, which makes thermalling the activity the class exists for rather than one skill among many. There's a second reason too: the point of a better-gliding wing is that it gives you more information, and that's only worth having if you can already use it. The suggestion below has specific things to drill.

source.cites: Seb Ospina via XC Mag (industry/expert): readiness means reading air well enough that a better-performing wing's extra feedback is actually useful rather than wasted. The thermic-hours figures from Hamerton via Cross Country Magazine, Flybubble and 406 Paragliding make thermic flying the measured activity for this step.
source.note: 'Not confident with it yet' and 'wide turns, losing the core' reach this rule. 'I mostly soar rather than thermal' scores 0.5, exactly on the minimum, so it passes here and is handled by 'unevidenced_core_checks' instead.

critical_check_floor:reading_the_day.message: One thing is holding this back: not yet being able to call the day yourself. Going when experienced pilots say it's good is a sensible way to fly and nobody should talk you out of it — but it means the judgement hasn't been built yet, and this is the step where the flying starts happening further from home, on days you chose, at sites you don't know as well. Worth knowing one instructor's own accident story here: a sudden collapse low over a sun-heated industrial roof on a day that looked benign from altitude. Reading the day includes reading the ground under it. It's a judgement skill, so it builds from conversation and attention as much as from airtime — the suggestion below has the drill.

source.cites: Simon Winkler via Podz-Glidz Episode 112 (expert, DHV instructor) describes his own frontal collapse in otherwise benign-feeling air while gliding low over a sun-heated industrial roof, and generalises a caution about heated and thermogenic ground surfaces producing sudden violent turbulence near the ground even on days that don't look rough from altitude. Hamerton via Cross Country Magazine (expert) frames this step as the point cross-country flying becomes the pilot's focus.
source.note: Only 'I mostly go when other people say it's good' reaches this rule. 'Right about half the time' scores exactly 0.5 and passes — no source gives an accuracy standard for reading a day at this step either, and treating an honest middling answer as disqualifying would invent one. This rule and reserve_familiarity are the two softest-sourced members of the list and sit late in its order for that reason.

critical_check_floor:active_piloting.message: One thing is holding this back: what your hands do when the air gets bumpy. Trying to react without it being automatic yet is an honest, common answer — it's held here because this is the one demand the manufacturers of these wings name explicitly. Their own description of the step up is that it asks more of the pilot specifically in turbulence. One DHV instructor puts the standard in useful detail: hands up on calm glides, light contact when it's mildly rough so you can feel the pressure change, down into the brake range to correct when it's working — and he's blunt that holding the brakes in one fixed position all the time is a false sense of security rather than a safe default. The habit builds much more easily on the wing that forgives it. There's a suggestion below with the drill.

source.cites: Advance via Flybubble (manufacturer via retailer): "a clear step up in demands on the pilot," specifically around doing the right things in turbulence; Gin via Flybubble matches. Simon Winkler via Podz-Glidz Episode 112 (expert, DHV instructor): hands fully up on calm glides, light contact position in mild turbulence, mid-brake-travel for active correction in thermic lift, and static light-brake flying explicitly discouraged.
source.note: 'Hands still', 'grip tight' and 'try to react' all reach this rule. 'I work the brakes to keep the pressure even' scores 0.7 and passes comfortably, even though it is marked down from 0.9 one rung below — the scoring change is a scoring change, not a block.

critical_check_floor:collapse_experience.message: One thing is holding this back, and it isn't that you froze — that's what most people do the first time, and it's the normal starting point rather than a character flaw. It's that the wing sorted itself out without you, so the reaction hasn't been tested. This step's guidance asks for collapses, wingovers and spirals as regular practice rather than theory by now, and there's a specific, practical reason to do it on the wing you've got: two instructors argue separately that wings much above this class resist collapsing so well that a course can't make the failure behave realistically, so the muscle memory has to be built lower down the ladder. Your current wing is close to the last good one for the job. There's a suggestion below.

source.cites: Flybubble's Reducing Risk (industry) recommends regular proactive practice of wingovers, spirals and asymmetric collapses around this stage, not just theoretical knowledge. knowledge/disagreements.md points 8 and 12: Greg Hamerton via FAI/CIVL (expert) recommends a manoeuvres clinic before pushing any wing's envelope; Simon Winkler via Podz-Glidz (expert, DHV instructor) argues that from roughly EN-C up, wings resist collapsing too strongly for realistic simulation, so the training has to happen earlier on lower-class wings.
source.note: Only 'I froze and the wing recovered on its own' reaches this rule; 'lost control' and 'happened a few times and I still struggle' fire the 'collapse_control_lost' gate, and 'never' scores 0.55 and passes. The two-instructor argument is the strongest claim this step has on the manoeuvres-course suggestion anywhere in the ladder, which is why it appears in the message rather than only in the suggestion.

critical_check_floor:collapse_practice.message: One thing is holding this back: collapses, wingovers and spirals as something you've read about rather than something you practise. That's the one place this step's guidance is more demanding than the step below it — one rung down, this is the skill you're expected to be acquiring; here it's the skill you're expected to have been practising. There's a practical reason to do it now rather than after the upgrade, made independently by two instructors: wings much above this class resist collapsing so well that a course struggles to make the failure realistic, so this is close to your last chance to build the reaction on a wing where it can be induced properly. Height, a calm day, someone watching the first few — the suggestion below has the order to do it in.

source.cites: Flybubble's Reducing Risk (industry): regular proactive practice of wingovers, spirals and asymmetric collapses around this stage, "not just theoretical knowledge". knowledge/disagreements.md points 8 and 12 for the two-instructor argument (Hamerton on compounding risk, Winkler on training feasibility above EN-C).
source.note: 'Not at all' and 'theory only' reach this rule; self-practised tip folds score 0.6 and pass. Deliberately not a gate — see meta.design_decisions 'v1-collapse-practice-becomes-a-ready-blocker'. The message explicitly names the difference from the step below, because a pilot who ran a low-B to high-B chain will have been told the opposite one screen earlier and deserves the reason.

critical_check_floor:reserve_familiarity.message: One thing is holding this back, and it's the quickest on the whole list to fix: not being certain you could find the reserve handle in a hurry. Two minutes in a hang check changes this answer permanently. It's the only item here that takes minutes rather than seasons, which is the one reason a single answer about it can hold an otherwise strong result. There's a suggestion below on how to practise it.

source.cites: USHPA P2 (official) includes reserve-deployment and PLF knowledge among its required skills.
source.note: Cross-referenced from two steps below: knowledge/steps/mid-b-to-high-b.md names no reserve criterion at all. Kept as a Ready-blocker on knowledge/disagreements.md point 5's conservative default, and flagged in this file as the weakest-sourced member of critical_check_floor.questions. The message avoids claiming a standard and leans on how cheap the fix is, which is the honest basis for it.

critical_check_floor:response_when_rough.message: One thing is holding this back, and it isn't nerves — everyone's heart rate climbs in rough air and that part is normal, not a weakness. It's what comes next: tightening up and waiting it out rather than carrying on flying the wing. That answer carries more weight here than any other mindset question, and more at this step than at the ones below it, because rough thermic air is the working environment this class of wing is actually sold for — its own makers describe the step up as asking more of you specifically in turbulence. What you do under load is a habit rather than a personality trait, so it builds. Until it feels different, the more forgiving wing is the right one to be building it on — there's a suggestion below on how.

source.cites: Advance via Flybubble (manufacturer via retailer) names the demand as doing the right things in turbulence; XC Mag's 'The Head Game' (industry/expert, featuring sports psychologist Thomas Theurillat) frames readiness as challenge matched to honest self-assessed skill, with too big a jump producing stress rather than growth.
source.note: Written about behaviour under load, not about feeling afraid, and deliberately does not reassure a hesitant pilot toward upgrading — the hesitation here is well-founded and the message says the forgiving wing is the right one for now. Required by docs/design-context.md; none of its terminology is used.

unevidenced_core_checks:thermal_turn_con.message: One thing is unevidenced rather than weak. You've said you mostly soar or glide rather than thermal, so the main thing this step is measured by hasn't been tested — and it isn't counted against you, it scores as neutral. But every source that puts a number on this step counts thermal hours specifically, and the wings in this class are described by their own makers as cross-country wings for turbulent thermic air. So unlike at the steps below this one, this result doesn't move just because your plans are local: there isn't a version of the guidance here that a soaring-only pilot clears. That's worth knowing plainly rather than discovering later. There's a suggestion below about what a high-B would and wouldn't give you for the flying you've described.

source.cites: "Convergent theme across manufacturer positioning (Advance, Gin, Nova) and Flybubble: high-B is explicitly for pilots moving into proper cross-country flying and more turbulent thermic air, not just bigger ridge days." All three hours figures measure thermic flying.
source.note: The third sentence is the pilot-facing form of thresholds.ready.unevidenced_core_checks.exemptions_deliberately_empty, and is the one message in this file that must change if the owner ever honours Hamerton's ridge route. Paired with the 'thermalling_untested' and 'local_plans_and_this_wings_purpose' suggestions, which carry the practical half.

ready_category_floor:skills.message: Your total is in the ready band, but the skills and experience half of it isn't carrying its own weight yet. The two halves are scored separately on purpose, so that good judgement and honest motives can't stand in for airtime and handling, or the other way round. What's holding this back is on the skills side, and the suggestions below are the specific parts of it.

source.cites: SAHPA's conservative-by-default pattern: when evidence is ambiguous, default toward 'Not yet' or 'Nearly ready' rather than 'Ready'.
source.note: Names the category rather than the floor value; the number would be false precision, since thresholds.ready.source records these figures as synthesised rather than sourced.

ready_category_floor:psychological.message: Your total is in the ready band, but the mindset and motivation half of it is sitting well below the skills half. Those are scored separately on purpose and they count for nearly as much: what you expect the new wing to actually do, what you're working on, how the call gets made on a marginal day, and what you do when it gets rough all matter here as much as hours and handling. At this step in particular, the guidance is unusually direct that a high-B is earned rather than aspired to, which is why this half can hold the result on its own. It's usually the quicker half to move.

source.cites: "Psychological answers carry real weight, not a side note." Plus knowledge/steps/mid-b-to-high-b.md#red-flags: Advance, Gin and Seb Ospina all flag aspirational buying in different words, and Hamerton via Cloudbase Mayhem 72 corroborates independently.
source.note: 'Usually the quicker half to move' is deliberate: these are answers that change with a conversation and some reading, not with another fifty hours — and saying so keeps the message from reading as a verdict on the pilot's character.

not_yet_category_floor:skills.message: Whatever the total came out at, the skills and experience answers point the same way: more flying on the wing you've already got is the useful next step, rather than a different wing. That's a normal place to be — this is the rung where the published guidance gets noticeably more demanding, and most pilots spend a couple of seasons on it. It's also the most fixable half of the picture: thermal hours, active flying, collapse practice and reading the day all move it, and every one of them transfers to whatever you fly next, so none of that time is spent waiting.

source.cites: "Hard gates: some answers ... cap the result at 'Not yet' regardless of total score." The category floors are the same idea applied to a whole category rather than a single answer.
source.note: Tone is bound by docs/design-context.md's safety guard: this must land as a legitimate, useful result, never as a failure. Hence 'a normal place to be' and 'the most fixable half'. The 'couple of seasons' framing is supported by knowledge/disagreements.md point 13 (every source addressing progression pace assumes one rung at a time) and point 10 (a community rule of thumb of 150-200 hours per wing-class step).

not_yet_category_floor:psychological.message: This one isn't about your hands. The answers about why the change, what you expect it to give you, what you're working on, how decisions get made on a day you're unsure about, and what's happened in the last year are where this result comes from — and here they count for nearly as much as hours and handling, by design. None of that is a judgement on you as a pilot. It's also the half the guidance for this step is most direct about: the people who build these wings write about them as something you move onto having run out of what you've got, not as a way to get there. It's the half worth working through first, and it usually takes a conversation with someone who knows your flying rather than another fifty hours in the air.

source.cites: Recommended handling: motivation is a genuinely scored input, and the diagnostic combination both camps agree on is an ambition- or comparison-flavoured motive paired with thin evidence of readiness elsewhere. knowledge/steps/mid-b-to-high-b.md#red-flags: Advance, Gin and Seb Ospina all flag aspirational buying; Hamerton via Cloudbase Mayhem 72 corroborates independently.
source.note: This is the more serious of the two floors — it produces Not yet rather than Nearly ready — so the tone constraint from docs/design-context.md is strictest here. 'None of that is a judgement on you as a pilot' is load-bearing and should not be cut: the answers that trip this floor (comparison-driven motives, launching under social pressure, unexplained near misses) are the ones most likely to read as character criticism if stated plainly. The message names the question areas without quoting any specific answer back at the pilot.

conservative_backstop.message: A few of the main questions were left blank, so there isn't quite enough here to put the result any higher than this. Nothing is counted against you for skipping them — when the tool doesn't know, it assumes the more cautious answer rather than the generous one. If you'd like a sharper result, going back and filling those in is the whole fix.

source.cites: SAHPA's design pattern of defaulting an unregistered glider to the most demanding category unless a lower class is actively registered. Applied here as: when the evidence is incomplete, default down rather than up.

rule_messages.fallback_purpose: Entries under 'fallback_by_rule_id' are used only when 'by_rule' has no entry for the exact fired-rule string — i.e. when a question is added to thresholds.ready.critical_check_floor.questions, or an answer to thresholds.ready.unevidenced_core_checks.answers, without per-case copy being written. They are intentionally vaguer than the per-question messages and should be treated as a bug signal, not a design target: if one of these ever renders, write the specific message.

critical_check_floor.message: One specific check for this step came out low, and a single weak answer in that group holds the result here even when everything else is strong — that's deliberate, so a good overall average can't cover one thin safety skill. The suggestions below name the one it was and what moves it.

unevidenced_core_checks.message: One of the checks for this step hasn't been tested rather than failed. The suggestions below cover how to test it while the stakes are low.

not_yet_category_floor.message: One of the two halves of this — skills and experience, or mindset and motivation — came out low enough that it decides the result on its own, whatever the total says. That's a normal result and a useful one: it means there's a specific half to work on rather than a vague sense of not being ready. The suggestions below are the concrete version.

always_output.instructor_recommendation: Whatever this says, run it past an instructor or coach who has seen you fly — and test-fly the specific wing before you buy it. That matters here because two of the manufacturers in this class describe their own high-B wings as being for pilots who are naturally talented or very current, which is not a judgement anyone can make about themselves from a form.
always_output.disclaimer: This is a self-assessment tool based on published guidance from national associations, manufacturers, retailers and instructors. It isn't an instructor, it can't see you fly, and it isn't a safety clearance. Wing choice is your responsibility and your instructor's advice always comes first.
always_output.methodology_note: This is one of the better-evidenced rungs on the ladder. Three sources land on roughly 50 hours of thermic flying before a high-B, and three manufacturers independently describe their high-B wings as not for beginners or occasional pilots. Two honest caveats: two of those three hours sources share an author, so the agreement is real but narrower than it looks; and the exact thresholds here are still our own synthesis, not a figure lifted from an authoritative table, because no such table exists. Where the sources disagreed — most visibly about whether ridge-soaring hours can substitute for thermic hours — we took the stricter reading. Every weight and gate links back to the criterion it came from.

source.cites: "A recommendation to discuss the upgrade with an instructor, plus a clear disclaimer."
source.note: Methodology wording follows knowledge/disagreements.md point 2's instruction to be explicit that thresholds are synthesised and point 6's instruction to keep confidence language a notch below 'three independent sources agree' wherever Hamerton/Flybubble material forms part of the count. It is more confident than low-B to mid-B's equivalent and more specific than A to low-B's, which matches the relative evidence.
